title: Ruling Out Polysemanticity With a Proxy
takeaway: A schematic of the paper's argument for specificity: if an independently computed proxy marks out a small, specific region of the data, and a feature only fires inside that region, then the feature cannot be firing on the mix of unrelated things that makes a neuron polysemantic. The third panel adds the paper's own caveat: a feature is often narrower than its proxy, with other features covering the rest.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Three cartoon panels, not plots of measured data. In each one the large grey circle stands for the whole set of tokens in the training distribution. Black dots mark tokens where a single learned [[feature]] is active. The orange ring, in the second and third panels, encloses the tokens that a [[computational-proxy]] flags as belonging to some hypothesized context.

The proxy is a score you can compute from the text alone: $\log(P(s\mid\text{context})/P(s))$, the log-likelihood ratio of a string under a hand-written model of the context against its likelihood under the empirical data distribution. Nothing about the autoencoder enters that number. That independence is the point — it gives a yardstick the learned feature was not fit to.

### How to read it

Read each panel as a question about overlap. Do the black dots sit inside the orange ring, or scatter across the grey circle?

Panel one is what [[polysemanticity]] looks like: one unit firing on several clearly unrelated kinds of input, dots spread with no common region.

Panel two is the case the paper wants. Every dot falls inside the ring, so whenever the feature is on, the proxy says the context is present. The paper calls this [[activation-specificity]], and treats it as the more important half of its case.

Panel three is the honest complication. The feature's dots cover only part of the ring, and a second, paler feature covers the rest. When features are finer-grained than the proxy, several of them share the territory — the paper's [[multiple-features-for-one-context]] observation.

### What it establishes

The figure is an argument shape, not evidence. It says what a specificity result would rule out; the actual numbers arrive later, when [[feature-activation]] is histogrammed against proxy score for particular features.

Two hedges belong with it. A proxy built from Unicode blocks or character sets has false negatives — shared punctuation, whitespace, tokens split mid-character — so dots outside the ring are not automatically polysemanticity. And the panels say nothing about the reverse direction, whether the feature fires everywhere in the ring.

terms.definition: The label on the large grey circle: the full set of tokens in the model's training distribution, drawn as the universe inside which everything else lives.
The label on the black dots: the tokens where one learned feature has a nonzero value. Each dot is a place in the data where the feature fires, not a magnitude.

The label on the orange ring: the region of the data that a cheaply computable score marks as belonging to the hypothesized context. Here it is drawn as a hard boundary, though the underlying score is continuous.
The caption inside the third panel's ring, marking that region as the one the proxy flags — the same orange region as in panel two, now shown containing more than one feature.
The label on the two overlapping dots in panel three: separate learned features that each cover part of the proxy's region and together fill it. The paper reports this for Arabic and base64.
The failure mode panel one depicts: a single unit responding to a mixture of clearly unrelated contexts, so no one interpretation covers when it fires.

The paper's proposed unit of interpretation — a direction in activation space with a scalar activation, recovered as one hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder rather than as a neuron of the transformer.

The proxy's actual definition, $\log(P(s\mid\text{context})/P(s))$: how much more likely a string is under a model of the context than under the data as a whole. The paper motivates the log form by noting features act linearly on logits, so they should be incentivized to track log-likelihoods.

A string — in practice a prefix of tokens ending at the token being scored. The paper maximizes the ratio over the different prefixes leading up to and including that token, since a feature's activation can depend on what preceded it.
The likelihood of the string under the full empirical data distribution, estimated as a unigram product $\prod_{t\in s}p(t)$ over token frequencies.
The likelihood of the string under a hand-built generative model of the hypothesized context — random draws from a character set, or a Unicode-block test combined with Bayes' rule.
The claim panel two supports: when the feature is on, the context is usually present. It is one of the five claims the paper tries to establish for each feature it studies in depth.
The converse claim, not shown here: when the context is present, the feature is usually on. Panel three is where its failures get patched by other features.
The worked instance of this scheme, $\log(P(s\mid\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$, built by checking whether characters fall in Arabic Unicode blocks.

numbers.meaning: The number of panels: the failure case (scattered polysemanticity), the target result (feature inside proxy), and the complication (several features sharing one proxy region).
Dots drawn in panels one, two and three. These are illustrative counts only — the figure is a schematic, and no count corresponds to a measured number of tokens or features.
The per-character probability the base64 proxy assigns to any character in [a-zA-Z0-9+/], modeling a base64 string as uniform draws from its 64-symbol alphabet.
The per-character probability the DNA proxy assigns to each of A, T, C and G, modeling a DNA sequence as uniform draws from four letters.

The tiny probability assigned to a character outside the context's alphabet, or to $P(\text{Arabic}\mid s)$ when $s$ contains any non-Arabic character. It makes the log-ratio collapse for off-context strings rather than going to $-\infty$.
Two of the Unicode blocks the Arabic proxy tests membership in. Working from block ranges is what makes the proxy cheap, and also what makes it miss shared punctuation and whitespace.

The share of training tokens that are Arabic script — from the Arabic case study, not printed in this figure. It is the size of the orange ring relative to the grey circle in that instance, and small rarity is what gives panel two its force.
The share of tokens on which the Arabic feature is active that are actually Arabic script. This is the measured version of panel two: most dots fall inside the ring, though not all.
How that 81% varies with activation strength — 25% when the feature is barely on, 98% above an activation of 5. Panel two's clean containment holds at high activations and degrades at low ones.
The activation level above which the Arabic feature's specificity reaches 98%. The paper argues large activations matter most because a feature's effect on the logits is linear in its activation.
